AKAF: Large companies spread across the world economy, with delivery firms, energy producers and travel names all prominent, and no single holding dominating. It is a broad growth holding: the even spread keeps one stock from driving returns, though it still swings with global markets.
AMMO: Companies in the defense supply chain, from weapons and vehicle makers to the parts and electronics suppliers behind them, mostly industrials with some technology. It is a focused bet on military spending: it rises and falls with defense budgets rather than the broad economy.
BCKT: US Treasury securities arranged to pay out a planned stream of income ending in 2030, with the schedule set in advance. It is an income planning tool for a known horizon: the fixed end date makes it act more like a maturing bond than an open-ended fund.
BCOR: Companies worldwide that hold bitcoin on their balance sheets, spread across technology, consumer, financial and media stocks. It offers stock-market exposure to bitcoin adoption without holding crypto directly, but its price still swings with both the stock market and bitcoin sentiment.
BFOC: Bitcoin exposure with a built-in floor, using options to limit losses over an outcome period that started in October while keeping some upside. It is a cautious way to hold a volatile asset: the floor softens drops, gains are capped, and terms reset each period.
BFXU: US large-cap stocks through a ladder of four accelerator funds with staggered outcome periods, designed to multiply moderate market gains up to a cap. The ladder spreads out start dates, but acceleration cuts both ways in timing: strong rallies are capped, and losses are not cushioned.
BPI: Bitcoin exposure built from options on bitcoin funds, structured to collect premium income while following bitcoin's price with a cap on gains. It is an income twist on a volatile asset: payouts come from option premiums, but the fund still falls when bitcoin drops.
CBTL: Bitcoin exposure through a ladder of structured protection funds with staggered one-year outcome periods, aiming to shield against losses while capping gains. Staggering the periods means some protection is always partway through its term, though the fund still moves with bitcoin between resets.
CBXL: Bitcoin exposure through a ladder of four structured protection funds with staggered outcome periods, built to limit downside while keeping capped upside. The ladder smooths the timing risk of a single outcome period, but it still falls with bitcoin and gains stop at each fund's cap.
CHDG: Shares of S&P 500 funds paired with options hedges the manager adjusts to soften market drops. It is a defensive core holding: the goal is to keep most of the market's upside while falling less in sell-offs, accepting that the hedging costs something in calm markets.
CROB: Chinese companies building robots and automation systems, from factory machines to humanoid and service robots. It is a narrow, high-risk theme bet on China's robotics push: the fund is concentrated in one country and one industry, so policy and market swings hit it hard.
DRAY: Options on a single stock, DraftKings, arranged to pay current income while following its share price up to a limit on gains. It is a concentrated income bet on one sports-betting company, so the payout stream comes with that stock's sharp price swings.
DVDN: Mortgage REITs and business development companies, firms that lend on homes, commercial property and private businesses and pass most of their earnings out as dividends. It is an income holding with credit risk: payouts can be high, but values swing when loans sour or rates jump.
DVVY: Large US companies that pay dividends, picked with an emphasis on spreading across sectors rather than chasing the highest yields. It is a classic equity income holding: dividends provide a steady payout stream, though the fund still moves with the stock market and can fall in sell-offs.
EMOT: S&P 500 companies screened for durable competitive advantages, using strong profit margins, returns on capital and market share, spread across technology, consumer and health care stocks. It is a quality tilt on a core holding: the screen favors entrenched businesses over the plain index.
FB: Large US stocks with an options buffer that resets daily, using one-day options to soften losses whenever the market falls. Unlike typical buffer funds with a fixed year-long period, this cushion is rebuilt every day, so protection is always fresh but never tied to a set outcome date.
GMEY: Options on a single stock, GameStop, arranged to pay current income while following its share price up to a limit on gains. It is a concentrated income bet on one of the market's most volatile meme stocks, so sharp swings come with the territory.
HALX: Companies with heavy physical assets and slow-changing businesses, led by utilities and energy at about a fifth each, plus industrials and consumer staples. It is a defensive value-leaning holding: asset-heavy firms tend to be steadier, but they can lag when growth stocks are in favor.
HAUG: S&P 500 exposure through options built to protect against losses over an outcome period that started in August, with gains capped in exchange for that protection. The August start matters: anyone buying later gets the remaining terms, not a fresh year of full protection.
HWSM: Small and mid-sized companies the manager judges undervalued, spread across financials, consumer, technology and industrial stocks. It is an actively managed value holding: the stock picking aims to find bargains in the market's middle tier, which tends to swing more than large companies.
IACL: Autocallable notes tied to the 100 largest US stocks, structured contracts that pay income and can end early if the market rises. It is an income holding with fine print: returns depend on the notes' terms, and losses arrive if the underlying stocks fall far enough.
KIQQ: Nasdaq stocks wrapped in a dynamic buffer strategy that aims for high income while cushioning part of any drop, with technology about 60% of the mix. It mixes growth and defense: the buffer softens losses in exchange for capped gains, and terms adjust as markets move.
LFAW: US Treasury securities arranged to pay out a planned stream of income through the year 2060, like a pension you can buy in a fund. It is built for very long-term income planning: payments are the point, and the distant end date sets it apart.
LGHT: Healthcare technology companies from around the world, from medical software and devices to digital health services, at any company size. It is a focused growth bet on medicine going digital: it can grow fast, but health tech swings with regulation and hospital spending.
LQ: A mix of alternative strategies beyond plain stocks and bonds, chosen with taxes in mind for investors in higher brackets. It is a diversifier meant to zig when markets zag, and its tax-aware design sets it apart from most alternative funds, which often create messy tax bills.
MEIB: Income built around a single stock, Meta Platforms, using an index of options and swaps designed to boost payouts from its price moves. It is a concentrated bet on one company: the strategy aims for income, but Meta's swings drive the result either way.
MLCC: Makers of multilayer ceramic capacitors and other electronic components, the tiny parts inside nearly every modern device, all within the technology sector. It is a narrow supply-chain bet: demand follows the global electronics cycle, so it can swing hard with chip and device sales.
MSEP: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged to give moderate protection against losses over an outcome period that started in September, with gains capped in exchange. It is a cautious equity holding: the September start date matters, because the protection terms were set then, not when you buy.
MTAW: Companies tied to Meta's artificial intelligence ecosystem, from technology and social media to the utilities that power data centers. It is a focused AI bet organized around one company's orbit: it captures suppliers and partners, not just Meta itself, and swings with the AI trade.
NVIB: Income built around a single stock, NVIDIA, using an index of options and swaps designed to boost payouts from its price moves. It is a concentrated bet on the chip giant: the income strategy cannot remove the sharp swings that come with one high-flying stock.
ODTE: Option premium income built on three big US stock indexes at once, the S&P 500, the Nasdaq-100 and the small-cap Russell 2000. It is an income strategy rather than a growth one: selling options pays regularly, but caps how much it gains when stocks climb.
OPPG: Companies around the world chosen using geopolitical analysis, spread across industrials, technology, consumer and media stocks. It is an actively managed global growth holding: the manager shifts toward countries and industries expected to benefit from world events, so results depend heavily on those calls being right.
PCSG: A focused portfolio of small and mid-sized growth companies, led by technology at about a third, with industrials and health care behind it. It is an actively managed growth holding: smaller companies offer more room to run, but they swing more than large stocks.
PEVC: Public stocks, funds and futures combined to mimic how private equity and venture capital portfolios perform, led by technology at nearly half. It is a growth holding for investors who want private-market style exposure they can trade daily, though the match to real private funds is only approximate.
PLIB: Income built around a single stock, Palantir, using an index of options and swaps designed to boost the payout from its price moves. It is a concentrated bet: everything depends on one company's stock, so it can swing sharply even though the goal is income.
PMTL: Mining companies that dig up gold, silver and other precious metals, screened for quality by profitability and balance-sheet measures. It is a leveraged-feeling bet on metal prices: miners usually rise faster than gold itself when prices climb, and fall harder when they drop.
PQXV: Large US stocks through options on the S&P 500, with a built-in cushion that absorbs the first 15% of losses over each quarterly outcome period. It is made for cautious stock investors: gains are capped, and the protection resets every three months rather than lasting all year.
QQLV: The calmest slice of the Nasdaq-100: the large stocks that swung the least over the past year, which tilts it toward consumer staples, industrials and utilities. It is a defensive growth holding, built to fall less in sell-offs while giving up some punch in rallies.
RKSG: US growth stocks picked by a rules-based screen, led by technology at about a third, with health care, financials and energy behind it. It is built for growth as a core equity holding, and its index rules, not a manager, decide what gets in or out.
STBQ: Companies building stablecoin technology and infrastructure, mostly financial firms with a large technology slice, plus some digital asset funds. It is a focused bet on dollar-linked crypto going mainstream: it swings with both payment stocks and crypto sentiment.
STLR: Exposure to Stellar's XLM crypto token through regulated futures contracts, backed by cash and high-quality collateral. It offers a way to trade XLM's price in a brokerage account without holding the token, but futures-based pricing can drift from the spot price and crypto swings are large.
TEXX: Texas-based companies, with energy firms making up about 70% of the fund and smaller stakes in industrial, consumer and utility businesses. It is a focused bet on one state's economy, so it rises and falls with Texas oil and gas more than a national fund would.
TORK: Companies that make actuators, the motors and motion parts that move machines, robots and vehicles, mainly industrials with some consumer names. It is a narrow robotics supply-chain bet: demand rides factory automation and electric vehicles, so it swings with manufacturing spending.
TSRS: Real estate investment trusts that earn most of their revenue in states that voted Republican in presidential elections, covering apartments, retail, offices and other property types. It is a politically themed property bet: the screen is about state politics, not property quality, so the mix is unusual.
TSYW: Leveraged exposure to long-term US Treasury bonds through swaps on a Treasury bond fund, structured to pay distributions every week. It is a short-term trading tool rather than a buy-and-hold bond fund: leverage magnifies moves, and bond prices fall when interest rates rise.
UFOD: Aerospace, defense and technology companies the manager believes would benefit if governments disclose or exploit technology from unidentified anomalous phenomena. It is a speculative theme bet: industrials are over half the fund, and returns hinge on a disclosure story that may never arrive.
VBNB: A single crypto asset, BNB, the token of the BNB Chain network, held directly by the trust. It is a pure price bet on one coin: there is no diversification and no income, so it swings with BNB alone and can move violently.
VOOY: Large US companies combined with options on large-cap stocks and indexes, built to turn part of the market's movement into income. It is an income-first equity holding: the options add regular payouts but limit how much it gains in strong rallies.
XLCI: Communication services stocks from the S&P 500, meaning telecom carriers, media companies and internet platforms, paired with an options overlay that sells options to add income. It targets income from a growth-heavy sector, giving up some upside when these stocks run hard.
XLRI: Real estate stocks from the S&P 500, mainly property owners and REITs, paired with an options overlay that sells options against them to generate extra income. It is an income-focused way to hold the property sector, trading some upside in strong rallies for regular option premium.
